topic.title: IRI regime collapse and formation of a new Iranian state

parties.name: Republic of Turkey
parties.description: Turkey has responded to the Iran crisis with controlled border management, defensive air-security measures, and active diplomacy. On 2 March 2026 Ankara kept commercial freight moving through the Gurbulak, Kapikoy, and Esendere crossings while mutually suspending daily passenger crossings with Iran; Turkish reporting also described reinforced personnel and control infrastructure. Reporting in March-April 2026 further indicated repeated missile-related incidents affecting Turkish airspace, reliance on NATO interception assets around sites such as Incirlik and Kurecik, and a policy line centered on de-escalation rather than war entry.
parties.agenda: Prevent uncontrolled spillover from Iran, keep the border and trade corridor functioning under tighter controls, protect Turkish territory and NATO-linked facilities from missile or debris incidents, and preserve a mediator role while resisting both regional escalation and Iranian fragmentation.
parties.means: ["selective border controls that can restrict passenger movement while preserving freight flows","rapid reinforcement of customs, personnel, and control infrastructure on the Iran border","access to NATO-linked air and missile defence architecture around strategic facilities","regional shuttle diplomacy and public positioning as a de-escalatory intermediary"]
parties.circle: {"visible":["unhcr","state_oman","nato","gulf arab states"],"shadow":["security coordination around Kurdish militant spillover and eastern-border surveillance","quiet deconfliction with Iran to prevent missile incidents or border escalation","behind-the-scenes balancing between Western allies and regional Muslim states to preserve mediation space"]}
parties.vulnerabilities: ["high domestic sensitivity to any new refugee influx from Iran","risk that missile interceptions or falling debris draw Turkey directly into the conflict","exposure of strategic sites such as Incirlik and Kurecik in a wider regional war","pressure from Kurdish spillover scenarios if Iranian state authority weakens near the border","difficulty maintaining neutrality while coordinating with NATO and engaging regional partners"]
parties.weight_evidence: {"military_capacity":"Turkey is a NATO member, giving it access to a 32-state military alliance (NATO member-states listing, 2025), and Ankara jointly restricted cross-border movement with Iran on 2 March 2026 while tightening border security in response to the Iran crisis (OSW, 5 March 2026, in the case context). SIPRI’s military expenditure database continues to track Turkish defense spending through 2024, indicating sustained major-force status even if Turkey is not a global top-tier power like the US or China.","economic_control":"Turkey has meaningful regional economic leverage through transit and border control, but its own macro position is constrained: Türkiye’s trade deficit widened to $11.3 billion in March 2026 (PA Turkey, 4 April 2026), and official inflation data showed CPI up 1.94% month-on-month and 30.87% year-on-year in March 2026 (Turkish Statistical Institute data reported 3 April 2026). Those figures limit Ankara’s ability to convert economic size into strong coercive leverage in an Iranian-collapse scenario.","information_control":"Domestically, Turkey retains substantial state leverage over the information space: Freedom House’s global freedom mapping continues to classify Turkey as only partly free/not free in key political-rights and internet-freedom measures, while RSF’s World Press Freedom Index map continues to place Turkey among poor press-freedom performers. That supports a middling-to-strong score for internal narrative control, but Turkey lacks the global information reach of the US, Russia, or China.","international_support":"Turkey’s diplomatic backing is strong because it sits inside NATO’s 32-member alliance and remains embedded in major Western institutions while also acting as a regional mediator. UNHCR data updated 5 April 2026 recorded more than 78,000 Iranians arriving in Türkiye since 28 February, and UNHCR’s broader refugee statistics continue to rank Türkiye among the world’s top refugee-hosting countries, reinforcing Ankara’s relevance to European, UN, and regional diplomacy.","internal_legitimacy":"President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan won reelection on 28 May 2023 for another five-year term (TIME, 28 May 2023), showing regime durability at the national level, but legitimacy is under strain. The opposition’s strong showing in the 31 March 2024 local elections was described as a major lesson for Erdoğan and the AKP (Al Jazeera Centre for Studies, 17 March 2026), and March 2026 inflation was still 30.87%, underscoring continued economic dissatisfaction."}

parties.name: European Iran Sanctions and Diplomatic Bloc
parties.description: European bloc centered on the EU, UK, and the E3 (France, Germany, UK) using layered sanctions, IAEA/UN nuclear diplomacy, and coordinated political messaging to constrain Iranian repression, proliferation, and regional destabilization. In 2026 it retained parallel EU and UK sanctions architectures, extended EU human-rights measures through 13 April 2027, and paired diplomatic pressure with defensive force-protection and energy-contingency measures during the regional war around Iran.
parties.agenda: Sustain coercive leverage over Iranian human-rights abuses, hostile activity, and nuclear escalation; preserve flexibility over sanctions relief and recognition in any post-IRI transition; avoid uncontrolled regional war while protecting European personnel, bases, shipping, and energy stability; keep the IAEA/UN track and E3 diplomacy central to any future settlement.
parties.means: ["EU sanctions regimes covering Iran human-rights abuses, WMD/non-proliferation, and military support networks","UK sanctions under the Iran (Sanctions) Regulations 2023 including financial, trade, immigration, and director-disqualification tools","asset freezes, travel bans, and export restrictions on internal-repression and telecom-monitoring equipment","E3 coordination through the IAEA Board of Governors and UNSCR 2231/snapback mechanisms","joint UK-France-Germany diplomatic statements shaping legitimacy and de-escalation messaging","defensive RAF and regional force-protection deployments rather than offensive warfighting","coordination with IEA partners on strategic petroleum releases and wider energy-security contingencies"]
parties.circle: {"visible":["European Union","United Kingdom","France","Germany","IAEA-linked E3 diplomatic channel"],"shadow":["member-state channels to Iranian technocrats, business intermediaries, and exile figures for transition sensing","quiet UK and European coordination with Gulf states on base security, shipping, and de-escalation","back-channel use of sanctions licensing and future relief as leverage over potential transitional authorities"]}
parties.vulnerabilities: ["member-state differences over escalation, recognition timing, and sanctions relief sequencing","limited direct coercive capacity inside Iran beyond sanctions, diplomacy, and external military posture","sanctions are blunt instruments if collapse creates humanitarian or migration emergencies","dependence on US military choices while preferring a more controlled diplomatic track","regional bases, shipping links, and energy markets remain exposed during Iran-related escalation","official messaging can overstate restraint while practical contingency involvement deepens","recognition and reconstruction policy would be fragmented between Brussels and national capitals"]
parties.weight_evidence: {"military_capacity":"This bloc is not a unified warfighting alliance, but it sits atop major European military capacity: NATO states that it is a 32-country alliance defending about 1 billion citizens, and nearly all EU members plus the UK are inside that structure. On the UK side specifically, reporting on 2026 NATO spending data says Britain spent £60.2 billion on defence in FY2024-25, giving the bloc real defensive reach even if its Iran policy tools are mainly sanctions and diplomacy.","economic_control":"The EU Sanctions Map in 2026 shows the EU operating three separate Iran sanctions regimes at once: human-rights measures, WMD/non-proliferation measures, and measures tied to Iran’s military support to Russia and armed groups in the Middle East/Red Sea. Those regimes include asset freezes, travel bans, dual-use export controls, telecom/internal-repression equipment restrictions, ports/vessels measures, and financial prohibitions—strong evidence of very high coercive economic leverage, especially when paired with the UK’s parallel sanctions architecture.","information_control":"The bloc has substantial intelligence and cyber coordination capacity but not full narrative dominance. Europol’s 2026 institutional structure includes the European Cybercrime Centre (EC3), European Counter Terrorism Centre (ECTC), Operational and Analysis Centre, SIENA secure information exchange, dedicated intelligence analysis, and an Innovation Lab—showing an extensive EU-wide information and cyber apparatus that can support sanctions enforcement and threat monitoring on Iran-related issues.","international_support":"The bloc aggregates the diplomatic weight of 28 European states (the 27-member EU plus the UK) and remains embedded in major multilateral channels. Most importantly on Iran, the World Nuclear Association’s 2026 update says the E3 (France, Germany, UK) triggered the UN snapback mechanism on 28 August 2025, reimposing all previous UN Security Council sanctions on Iran, demonstrating real ability to mobilize international institutions rather than act only unilaterally.","internal_legitimacy":"Cohesion is meaningful but not absolute. Eurobarometer’s December 2025 findings say 74% of respondents believed their country had benefited from EU membership, 48% trusted the EU, and 67% agreed the EU is a place of stability in a troubled world. On Iran specifically, the Council extended EU human-rights sanctions on Iran until 13 April 2027 in March 2026, indicating continued member-state unity behind the bloc’s sanctions line."}

parties.name: United States-Israel Alignment
parties.description: The United States-Israel alignment has moved from coercive pressure to direct joint military action against Iran in 2026. Open-source reporting indicates the two states initiated strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026 and were still conducting joint operations in early April, while U.S. negotiating positions reportedly paired maximal nuclear rollback demands with only limited sanctions relief. This makes the alignment decisive not only in degrading Iran’s nuclear and missile infrastructure, but also in determining whether any successor Iranian state gains sanctions relief, recognition, and access to the Western financial system.
parties.agenda: Prevent any successor Iranian state from reconstituting a nuclear weapons option, long-range missile threat, or proxy warfare architecture; force dismantlement or external control over sensitive nuclear assets; retain leverage over sanctions relief and international recognition; and shape a post-IRI order that is weaker, more surveilled, and less capable of regional revisionism.
parties.means: ["direct joint or coordinated U.S.-Israeli air and missile strikes on Iranian military, command, and nuclear-linked targets","maximalist diplomatic demands including dismantlement of major nuclear facilities and transfer of enriched uranium out of Iranian control","control over sanctions relief through U.S. Treasury, OFAC, and the wider dollar-clearing and shipping-access system","intelligence fusion, targeting support, and persistent surveillance of Iranian state and security structures","diplomatic coordination with Western and regional partners to shape legitimacy, reconstruction access, and post-conflict recognition","pressure on Iran’s oil export, shipping, and sanctions-evasion networks"]
parties.circle: {"visible":["us_ofac - central U.S. sanctions authority and practical gatekeeper for any Iranian reintegration into global finance","iaea - external verification body whose findings frame nuclear rollback demands and international justification debates","u.s. national security and diplomatic channels - reported to have advanced dismantlement and uranium-transfer demands in 2026 talks","israeli defense establishment - operational strike partner contributing targeting, airpower, and intelligence penetration"],"shadow":["possible back-channel outreach to Iranian elites and security defectors around post-regime or post-war arrangements","possible targeting and assessment networks inside Iran used for strike support and succession mapping","quiet coordination with regional states on airspace, basing, maritime security, and containment of retaliation"]}
parties.vulnerabilities: ["direct foreign military action can trigger nationalist backlash inside Iran and discredit domestic opposition as externally aligned","legal and legitimacy challenges are growing, with public expert criticism of the campaign’s international-law basis","civilian-site damage or perceived dual-use targeting can raise diplomatic costs and constrain coalition durability","maximalist rollback demands combined with minimal relief can impede stabilization even after regime weakening or collapse","the alignment still depends on limited U.S. and allied tolerance for prolonged war, economic shock, and regional escalation","Iran may still retaliate through proxies, missile attacks, maritime disruption, or asymmetric actions despite damage to its core infrastructure","overreach could push other external actors to provide Iran or successor hardliners with diplomatic, technical, or sanctions-evasion support even if they avoid formal military backing"]
parties.weight_evidence: {"military_capacity":"The bloc combines the world’s largest military with Israel’s high-intensity regional strike force. The New York Times reported on 2026-04-03 that the White House’s FY2027 request sought roughly $1.5 trillion for the U.S. military, while Israel’s 2026 defense budget was set at 112 billion shekels ($34.63 billion) according to the Israeli defense minister’s office as reported by Asharq Al-Awsat on 2025-12-05. Operationally, the New York Times reported on 2026-03-06 that Israel had begun a 'broad-scale' attack in Tehran and the Pentagon said Iran had retaliated with missile strikes.","economic_control":"The alliance has exceptional coercive economic leverage mainly through Washington’s control of sanctions and finance. OFAC’s official site states it 'administers and enforces economic and trade sanctions,' and Treasury-linked reporting in October 2025 said the U.S. sanctioned more than 50 individuals, entities, and vessels for facilitating Iranian oil and LPG exports. OECD’s Interim Economic Outlook (2026-03-23) said the Middle East conflict had already caused global energy and commodity prices to spike and increased financial-market volatility, underscoring the bloc’s ability to affect shipping and energy flows.","information_control":"The U.S.-Israel bloc has strong but not absolute information dominance through state institutions, intelligence systems, and agenda-setting media reach. OFAC and White House channels provide authoritative sanctions and war-policy signaling, while the conflict was being covered in real time by top global outlets such as the New York Times’ 2026 live war coverage; CSIS’s 'Significant Cyber Incidents' tracker also reflects the mature cyber battlespace in which U.S. and Israeli capabilities are major reference points. The limitation is that narrative control is contested internationally and in digital spaces.","international_support":"The alignment sits atop extensive U.S.-led alliance networks and still has substantial Western diplomatic weight, but support is not uniform. The U.S. remains the core power inside NATO and wider Western institutions, and UK-linked reporting referenced a parliamentary briefing describing U.S.-Israeli strikes beginning on 2026-02-28. At the same time, The War Zone reported on 2026-04-02 that 'key allies' were distancing themselves further from the Iran campaign, showing meaningful but not unanimous external backing.","internal_legitimacy":"As an alliance, cohesion is solid operationally but politically uneven. The two states were still acting jointly in March 2026 according to multiple war reports, and Israel’s defense and finance ministries agreed a 112 billion shekel 2026 defense framework despite broader wartime strain. However, the need for ongoing cabinet bargaining in Israel and the polarized U.S. domestic environment reduce the bloc’s internal political legitimacy relative to its hard-power capacity."}

parties.name: Islamic Republic Regime Continuity Bloc
parties.description: The Islamic Republic Regime Continuity Bloc remains the core survival coalition of Iran’s clerical-security state, centered on the Supreme Leader’s system, the IRGC, Basij, and aligned coercive institutions. Recent evidence reinforces that its power rests on a hybrid architecture: IRGC-led proxy and expeditionary networks, ballistic-missile and anti-shipping capabilities, coercive control over strategic chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz, and sanctions-evasion revenue channels that help finance repression, proxy warfare, and weapons procurement.
parties.agenda: Preserve the Islamic Republic’s command structure through coercive control, succession management, and refusal of externally imposed dismantlement; retain missile, enrichment, and proxy leverage; protect regime financing networks; and use maritime and regional escalation to raise the cost of pressure or regime-change efforts.
parties.means: ["command over IRGC military arms and associated proxy networks used for external power projection and internal regime defense","ballistic missiles, anti-ship missiles, naval mines, and small-boat swarm tactics that can threaten U.S. partners and disrupt Strait of Hormuz traffic","Basij-linked and internal-security repression capacity financed in part through opaque state and para-state revenue networks","shadow-fleet and shipping-company ecosystems used to generate revenue under sanctions pressure","control or influence over strategic nuclear and energy infrastructure, including Bushehr and broader state nuclear planning","hardline negotiating posture defending nuclear facilities, domestic enrichment, and broad sanctions relief as regime red lines","ability to weaponize maritime chokepoints and regional instability for economic and political leverage"]
parties.circle: {"visible":["IRGC and Qods Force command structures that connect state military power with partner militias and proxy forces","formal state institutions handling nuclear policy, sanctions negotiation, and strategic infrastructure","maritime-security and naval organs able to enforce or threaten closure of the Strait of Hormuz"],"shadow":["shadow-fleet vessels and affiliated shipping firms that help move revenue outside normal sanctions channels","procurement and financing networks supporting missile and drone programs","informal regional partner and militant networks used for deniable coercion and indirect retaliation"]}
parties.vulnerabilities: ["heavy dependence on sanctions-evasion shipping and opaque commercial networks that remain sanctionable and targetable","exposure of Hormuz coercion strategy to U.S. and allied naval countermeasures if maritime closure becomes unsustainable","continued reliance on unpopular repression, which deepens legitimacy deficits and increases risk if coercive cohesion weakens","sensitivity of strategic nuclear and military infrastructure to repeated external strikes","economic strain from disrupted shipping, sanctions pressure, and higher war-risk costs that can reduce patronage capacity","dependence on maintaining elite unity across clerical, IRGC, and security institutions during crisis succession or wartime stress"]
parties.weight_evidence: {"military_capacity":"CSIS’s Missile Threat update (3 Mar 2026) says Iran has 'the largest and most diverse missile arsenal in the Middle East,' with 'thousands of ballistic and cruise missiles' and an active record of supplying missiles and UAS to Hezbollah, Iraqi militias, the Houthis, and Russia. During the 2026 war, Al Jazeera (8 Mar 2026) reported the IRGC was still conducting the '27th wave of Operation True Promise' and striking Israel and Gulf-state targets despite major US-Israeli attacks, indicating substantial residual deterrent and strike capacity.","economic_control":"Iran’s direct economy is constrained, but it still retains meaningful coercive energy leverage: Al Jazeera (8 Mar 2026) reported that the Strait of Hormuz was 'effectively shut' during the war and that Brent crude rose 27% in one week, showing Iran can still disrupt globally significant oil flows. The World Bank’s GDP database lists Iran with current-dollar national accounts coverage through recent years, confirming a sizable state economy, but sanctions and wartime damage sharply limit the bloc’s ability to convert that base into broad economic power.","information_control":"Freedom House’s Freedom in the World 2026 report gives Iran 0/4 on whether media are free and independent, saying state broadcasting is tightly controlled, critics are excluded, and 'tens of thousands' of foreign websites are filtered while satellite broadcasts are jammed. The same 2026 report states that during the June war authorities imposed an internet shutdown, tightened censorship, and required media to 'observe and respect redlines,' while also using SIM-card deactivations to punish critical online speech.","international_support":"The bloc retains a real but mostly non-state external network: CSIS (3 Mar 2026) says Iran supplies missiles, rockets, and UAS to partners and proxies in Iraq, Lebanon, the Palestinian territories, Yemen, and Russia. But state-level diplomatic backing appears weak: Al Jazeera (8 Mar 2026) reported the GCC condemned Iran’s attacks as 'dangerous acts of aggression,' and the Arab League said attacks on member states 'cannot be justified,' indicating regional isolation rather than a strong formal coalition.","internal_legitimacy":"Freedom House 2026 describes a new nationwide protest wave from late December 2025 driven by 'soaring inflation' and a 'collapsing currency,' with security forces using force and threats of harsh punishment to disperse demonstrators; it also cites a UN fact-finding mission finding at least 551 protesters were killed in the 2022 crackdown. Yet the regime’s institutional durability remains significant: Al Jazeera (8 Mar 2026) reported a US National Intelligence Council assessment that even a 'large-scale' assault was unlikely to topple the government and that a fragmented opposition was unlikely to take control."}

parties.name: Iranian Reformist, Republican Diaspora, and Anti-War Left Bloc
parties.description: A clearer picture from April 2026 shows this bloc as a real but fragmented anti-war, non-monarchist current spanning diaspora advocacy infrastructure and republican-nationalist opposition networks. Its strongest documented components include NIAC’s diaspora lobbying and mobilization apparatus around peace-and-diplomacy campaigning, and National Front organizations abroad that publicly opposed the U.S.-Israeli war while also rejecting Islamic Republic authoritarianism and calling for a constituent assembly, free elections, and a new constitution decided by Iranians rather than foreign-backed transition schemes.
parties.agenda: To stop foreign war and coercive regime engineering, resist monarchist or externally dependent transition projects, and push a domestically negotiated post-IRI order based on free elections, a constituent assembly, civil liberties, and a new constitution.
parties.means: ["diaspora advocacy infrastructure with chapters, membership, events, donation networks, congressional scorecards, and anti-war campaigns","public opinion shaping through diaspora media, statements, polling, and issue trackers focused on war, diplomacy, and civil-rights impacts","republican-nationalist statement networks such as National Front organizations abroad calling for ceasefire, negotiations, and constituent politics","political framing that simultaneously blames the Islamic Republic for the crisis and rejects foreign-imposed transition or anti-democratic opposition currents","lobbying in U.S. and European policy spaces for de-escalation, humanitarian protection, and diplomacy rather than military overthrow"]
parties.circle: {"visible":["National Iranian American Council and related anti-war Iranian-American advocacy spaces","National Front of Iran organizations abroad and Jebhe Melli Europe networks","European and transatlantic policy circles open to ceasefire, diplomacy, and non-monarchist transition formulas"],"shadow":["inside-Iran reformist and pragmatic networks that may share opposition to war without fully sharing diaspora republican agendas","state-continuity nationalist elements wary of both foreign attack and monarchist restoration","other republican and left anti-intervention exile currents that cooperate tactically on anti-war messaging"]}
parties.vulnerabilities: ["heavy fragmentation between Iranian-American advocacy groups, secular republicans, reformists, nationalists, and left anti-war actors","limited coercive power inside Iran compared with armed state institutions, security organs, and foreign-backed opposition organizations","reliance on advocacy and messaging tools means influence is stronger in discourse and lobbying than in territorial or security control","exposure to accusations of softness toward the Islamic Republic because they oppose foreign military intervention and rapid externally managed regime change","competing anti-IRI opposition brands, especially monarchist networks, can overshadow their messaging and fundraising reach","many of the bloc’s visible platforms are openly political advocacy outlets, which can reduce credibility with hostile audiences even when their organizational infrastructure is real"]
parties.weight_evidence: {"military_capacity":"This is a non-state political current with no identified armed wing, defense budget, or weapons systems; the bloc’s documented means are political networks, media campaigns, civil-society mobilization, and lobbying rather than force. In practical terms, that leaves it with virtually no independent coercive or deterrent capability compared with armed state and militia actors.","economic_control":"No current evidence shows this bloc controlling state revenues, sanctions policy, banking channels, or hydrocarbon infrastructure. Its leverage is indirect and advocacy-based; by contrast, Iran’s oil sector and macroeconomic levers remain in state hands, so this current has little direct capacity to allocate resources or shape the wartime economy.","information_control":"Freedom House’s 2026 Iran country report scores Iran at 11/100 overall freedom, and its 2025 Freedom on the Net report scores Iran’s internet freedom at 13/100, showing a highly restrictive information environment that sharply limits opposition and reformist messaging inside the country. The bloc does have some diaspora media and advocacy reach, but the available data point to structural weakness against state censorship rather than narrative dominance.","international_support":"The bloc has no treaty allies or formal recognition as a government-in-waiting, but it does benefit from a limited diplomatic opening: Oman remained an active mediation channel, with Channel NewsAsia on Feb. 27, 2026 reporting 'significant progress' in Oman-mediated U.S.-Iran talks. That suggests some receptivity in de-escalation-oriented diplomatic circles, especially in Oman and parts of Europe, but not a broad interstate coalition behind this current.","internal_legitimacy":"Reuters reported on Mar. 2, 2024 that Iran’s parliamentary-election turnout fell to about 41%, a historic low that signaled deep public discontent with the political order. At the same time, reformist-backed Masoud Pezeshkian won the 2024 presidential runoff after a first round in which he led with 44% and then prevailed in the runoff, showing that reformist branding still retains some social appeal; however, the low-turnout environment and loose coalition structure mean this bloc’s legitimacy is real but limited rather than dominant."}

parties.name: NCRI / PMOI-MEK under Maryam Rajavi + Party of Free Life of Kurdistan (PJAK)
parties.description: This opposition pole combines two very different anti-Islamic Republic vectors: the NCRI/PMOI-MEK’s exile-based transition project under Maryam Rajavi and PJAK’s Kurdish insurgent-political relevance in Iran’s northwest. Recent evidence reinforces that the NCRI is still promoting one of the clearest publicly articulated post-collapse blueprints—a provisional government limited to six months followed by Constituent Assembly elections under Rajavi’s Ten-Point framework—while PJAK remained politically active in 2026, including public messaging during Kurdish unrest and the March 2026 cross-border crisis. However, most hard evidence on NCRI structure and capacity remains self-reported, and neither branch shows verified national command over territory or state institutions inside Iran.
parties.agenda: Position itself as a ready-made post-IRI alternative by pairing an NCRI-led transitional political framework at the national level with PJAK-linked Kurdish leverage in the northwest, while seeking to convert unrest or state weakening into bargaining power, political recognition, and influence over constitutional redesign.
parties.means: ["exile-based political coalition branding centered on Maryam Rajavi’s Ten-Point Plan","public advocacy for a provisional government capped at six months before Constituent Assembly elections","diaspora lobbying and media amplification through NCRI-aligned channels and supportive foreign politicians","claimed internal activist/resistance networks inside Iran, though scale remains unverified","organizational infrastructure outside Iran, including the Albania-based Ashraf-3 hub","PJAK’s Kurdish militant-political networks and media apparatus","ability to mobilize or support strikes and unrest in Kurdish-populated areas","cross-border positioning within the broader PKK-linked Kurdish ecosystem"]
parties.circle: {"visible":["Maryam Rajavi as the NCRI’s principal public face and advocate of the provisional-government roadmap","NCRI/FAC spokesmen and allied diaspora messaging channels promoting the transition plan internationally","PJAK’s public political/media organs, including official statements on developments in Iranian and Iraqi Kurdistan"],"shadow":["claimed PMOI/MEK Resistance Units and clandestine supporters inside Iran","PJAK-aligned armed cadres and facilitators in Kurdish border zones","broader PKK-linked militant networks that could shape PJAK’s manpower, sanctuary, or escalation options in a vacuum scenario"]}
parties.vulnerabilities: ["NCRI claims about membership, overseas associations, and support base are largely self-reported rather than independently verified","MEK/NCRI legitimacy inside Iran remains highly contested and polarizing","no verified unified command structure links NCRI exile leadership with PJAK’s armed Kurdish networks","limited demonstrated control over territory, coercive institutions, or nationwide armed force","PJAK faces pressure not only from Tehran but also from Turkey because of PKK linkages","cross-border Kurdish militarization could trigger external intervention that constrains PJAK expansion","the coalition logic is strategically plausible in collapse scenarios but organizationally fragmented in practice","foreign governments may engage the transition rhetoric rhetorically without granting formal recognition or operational backing"]
parties.weight_evidence: {"military_capacity":"The PMOI/MEK is not fielding a recognized standing army today; available background material indicates it was an armed group until 2003 and then shifted to political activity. On the PJAK side, ISW reported on 8 January 2026 that PJAK was one of the Kurdish opposition groups able to call for and support a nationwide general strike in Iran’s Kurdish areas, showing some coercive and mobilization capacity but not large-scale conventional force projection.","economic_control":"I found no evidence that the NCRI/PMOI-MEK or PJAK controls meaningful state revenue, major natural resources, banking channels, or sanctioned trade flows in 2026. Their leverage is political and insurgent rather than economic, so their direct ability to shape a post-collapse Iranian economy appears negligible.","information_control":"Maryam Rajavi is still able to project a coherent transition narrative internationally: an Iran Freedom report on 1 March 2026 carried her message for the 'transitional period,' and a 7 February 2026 Berlin demonstration plus a 2026 International Women’s Day conference were publicized around her Ten-Point Plan. But I found no hard evidence of mass domestic media penetration, broadcast infrastructure, or cyber/intelligence capabilities comparable to a state actor.","international_support":"The NCRI retains access to sympathetic Western lawmakers and former officials, including a U.S. Congress-hosted conference on 10 September 2024 highlighted by NCRI media and continuing European demonstrations in 2026 around Rajavi’s platform. However, I found no evidence of formal state recognition of an NCRI government-in-waiting, while PJAK’s PKK linkage is a liability because Turkey’s Foreign Ministry notes the PKK is listed as a terrorist organization by the EU, United States, Canada, and Australia.","internal_legitimacy":"The bloc has a more structured transition blueprint than many exile rivals: Rajavi publicly advanced a provisional framework and six-month transition concept in early 2026. But its domestic mandate remains weak and contested; Politico reported on 24 February 2026 that many Iranians were increasingly looking to Reza Pahlavi as an opposition focal point, underscoring that NCRI/MEK is far from hegemonic inside Iran despite its organizational discipline."}

parties.name: China and Russia
parties.description: China and Russia remain important but asymmetrical external pillars around Iran. China’s leverage is primarily economic: the 2021 25-year cooperation framework, its role as Iran’s largest trading partner, and reporting that it absorbs most Iranian oil exports give Beijing major revenue and sanctions-evasion influence. Russia’s leverage is more security-political: its January 2025 20-year strategic partnership treaty with Iran institutionalized trade, intelligence, and military-security cooperation, but without a mutual-defense clause. During the 2026 Iran war, both favored diplomacy and regime continuity over a pro-Western realignment, yet available reporting also showed clear limits to their willingness or ability to directly rescue Tehran militarily.
parties.agenda: Preserve influence in any Iranian transition by blocking a decisive U.S.-Israeli strategic realignment, maintaining Chinese access to energy and commercial networks, and retaining Russian security, intelligence, and diplomatic relevance through a successor order that is pragmatic, non-West-aligned, and open to continued sanctions-circumvention ties.
parties.means: ["Chinese oil purchasing power and trade networks that sustain Iranian state revenue","Long-term China-Iran cooperation mechanisms from the 2021 comprehensive plan","Russian security, intelligence, and military-technical channels institutionalized in the 2025 partnership treaty","Use of national-currency and sanctions-evasion payment arrangements","UN and diplomatic positioning against Western military escalation or coercive transition frameworks","Mediation and de-escalation offers designed to preserve influence without direct intervention","Backchannel access to Iranian state, military, and bureaucratic elites through longstanding state relationships"]
parties.circle: {"visible":["Islamic Republic regime-continuity institutions in Tehran","Sultanate of Oman as a possible intermediary for de-escalation and crisis messaging","Republic of Turkey and Gulf states as regional interlocutors in any containment or transition diplomacy","Senior Pakistani officials as occasional diplomatic partners in China-backed regional peace messaging"],"shadow":["Islamic Republic Army and other order-preserving Iranian security elites who may matter in a managed transition","Iranian commercial intermediaries, shipping actors, and sanctions-evasion networks tied to Chinese trade","Russian intelligence and security intermediaries connected to treaty-era cooperation with Tehran","Chinese state-linked firms and financial facilitators that can preserve access even if formal politics shift"]}
parties.vulnerabilities: ["China and Russia have overlapping but not identical priorities: Beijing prioritizes commercial stability, while Moscow may value geopolitical disruption and anti-Western leverage","China’s Iran influence is economically deep but politically brittle if a nationalist post-IRI government rejects legacy deals","Russia’s treaty with Iran lacks a mutual-defense clause, exposing limits to direct military rescue expectations","Both powers have weak popular legitimacy inside Iran and risk backlash if identified with regime-continuity forces","War, sanctions, and shipping disruption can degrade the practical value of Chinese oil and trade leverage","Neither power appears well positioned to mount a trusted multinational stabilization effort inside Iran","A rapid pro-sovereignty transition in Tehran could seek diversified external ties and reduce dependence on both Beijing and Moscow"]
parties.weight_evidence: {"military_capacity":"Russia planned to expand its active military personnel to 1.5 million by the end of 2024, which would make it the second-largest active force after China, and ISW was still publishing Russian offensive campaign assessments in March 2026 showing sustained warfighting capacity. China was also ranked 2nd globally in 2025 military power in the 2025 Military Power Rankings search result, so together they remain a top-tier military pairing.","economic_control":"China remains the world’s second-largest economy, while the search results identified Russia as the world’s ninth-largest economy by nominal GDP. Beyond sheer size, both anchor non-Western economic coordination through the expanded 10-member BRICS grouping that now includes Iran (The Diplomat, 2026-04-03), giving them trade, payments, and sanctions-circumvention leverage relevant to any Iranian transition.","information_control":"Both states have strong state-directed information and intelligence systems, and current conflict reporting shows operational reach: ISW’s Iran update of 2026-03-11 said Russia had provided Iran with locations of U.S. military assets, while the same report said China continued supplying missile-fuel precursors to Iran. That does not equal narrative dominance inside Iran, but it shows meaningful intelligence, covert-support, and messaging capacity.","international_support":"China and Russia are two of the five permanent UN Security Council members with veto power, which gives them direct blocking power over coercive UN action (UN Security Council explainer cited in search results, 2025-06-05). The bloc’s leverage remains substantial through oil market weight, export-routing alternatives, financing capacity, and close coordination with U.S.-backed maritime and air-defense frameworks, but its infrastructure and trade arteries remain acutely vulnerable to missile, drone, and maritime coercion.
parties.agenda: Shape any post-IRI transition toward a non-revolutionary Iranian state that halts attacks on Gulf energy and civilian infrastructure, abandons proxy warfare, restores secure navigation through Hormuz, and becomes a sovereign state that can be engaged economically rather than contained militarily.

parties.weight_evidence: {"military_capacity":"Saudi Arabia remains the bloc’s military anchor: SIPRI’s latest published data put Saudi military spending at roughly $75-80 billion annually, placing it among the world’s top defense spenders, and the alliance is reinforced by advanced air and missile defense assets in Saudi and the UAE. clue_versions.bias_corrected_summary: A 4 April 2026 statement published by Melliun, the outlet of National Front organizations abroad and National Front of Iran–Europe, demanded an immediate halt to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, which it said violated international law. The statement called for serious peace negotiations, transfer of power to the people's real representatives, unconditional release of all political prisoners, end to executions, free elections under universally accepted supervision, and formation of a genuine constituent assembly to draft a new constitution. The statement blamed the Islamic Republic as the primary cause of the war through 47 years of anti-national policies, while also condemning foreign aggression and explicitly distinguishing Iranian national interests from those of Israel and the U.S. It warned that foreign forces and their dependents—especially advocates of foreign military intervention—can never have a place among the Iranian nation. clue_versions.bias_corrected_summary: The DIA's 2019 unclassified Iran Military Power assessment described Tehran's reliance on the IRGC, especially the Qods Force, to project power through a network of state and non-state partners while using ballistic missiles, naval mines, antiship missiles, and swarms of small boats to deter stronger adversaries and threaten Gulf shipping as part of a regime-survival strategy. This architecture was put to the ultimate test in late February–March 2026 when a joint US-Israeli campaign (Operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion) launched full-scale air operations across Iran. The campaign killed Supreme Leader Khamenei and senior officials on 28 February 2026, struck approximately 200 air defense systems, destroyed 17 Iranian warships including a submarine, and heavily targeted ballistic missile launchers, drone sites, military airfields, hardened underground facilities, IRGC bases, and internal security installations across at least 26 of 31 provinces. However, the proxy network (Hezbollah, Hamas, Iraqi militias, Houthis) had already been significantly weakened by prior operations. Analysis from Small Wars Journal, ACLED, and ISW indicates the regime faces an existential fight for survival but has not yet collapsed, with hardline IRGC elements dominating decision-making. The campaign has severely degraded but not eliminated the military architecture described in the 2019 DIA report, and the regime retains limited capability to disrupt Gulf shipping and internal security capacity to suppress dissent.

clue_versions.bias_corrected_summary: The UK Iran (Sanctions) Regulations 2023 statutory guidance, last updated 25 March 2026, remains in force imposing financial, trade, immigration, and director-disqualification sanctions administered across FCDO, OFSI, and the Office of Trade Sanctions Implementation. The regime's stated purposes are to encourage Iranian compliance with international human rights law and to deter hostile activity by Iran or Iran-backed armed groups. It overlaps with a separate Iran nuclear sanctions regime. However, since late March/early April 2026, the geopolitical context has shifted significantly: a US-Iran military conflict has erupted, with US strikes on Iran and Iran blocking the Strait of Hormuz. The UK and allies are now reportedly discussing additional sanctions to pressure Iran into reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and the House of Commons Library has published analysis on Iran in 2026 referencing plans for new sanctions and the debate on proscribing the IRGC. The EU also renewed its Iranian sanctions regime until 13 April 2027 at the end of March 2026. The existing UK sanctions framework may therefore be supplemented with further measures in the near term.

clue_versions.bias_corrected_summary: The original clue (March 18, 2026) noted that China's leverage in an Iran crisis rested on buying 80%+ of Iran's oil exports, Russian oil imports (~20% of China's energy), ~900 million barrels in strategic reserves, and ~46 million barrels of Iranian crude in tankers near the South China Sea. Since then, the Iran war (Operation Epic Fury, launched Feb 28, 2026) and Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz (selective blockade since March 15) have dramatically tested and partially overwhelmed these buffers. Updated figures from a House Select Committee on China report and Kpler tanker tracking show China was importing 1.38 million bpd of Iranian crude in 2025 (12% of total imports), with sanctioned oil accounting for one-fifth of total imports. China's strategic petroleum reserves are now estimated at ~1.39 billion barrels (as of March 2, 2026) — significantly higher than the original ~900 million barrel estimate — providing ~120 days of import cover. However, the Hormuz closure removed ~12 million bpd from global supply (per IEA), Brent surged past $126/bbl, and Asian LNG spot prices spiked 140%. Despite the larger-than-expected reserve buffer, China was forced into a major strategic concession: resuming large-scale purchases of US crude (~600,000 bpd / ~18 million barrels per month worth ~$10 billion) and US LNG, reversing its 2025 policy of halting US energy imports. Analysts interpret this as evidence that China's commercial buffering tools — while substantial — proved structurally inadequate against a prolonged Hormuz closure and the permanent loss of Iranian supply reliability. The original clue's thesis that China's tools are 'commercial buffering, stockpiles and trade networks rather than force projection' remains accurate in characterizing the nature of China's leverage, but events have shown these tools were insufficient to prevent a forced reorientation toward US energy dependence.

clue_versions.bias_corrected_summary: On 2026-03-12, U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright confirmed the United States would release 172 million barrels of oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) as part of the International Energy Agency's coordinated effort to release 400 million barrels from member nations' emergency reserves — the largest such release in IEA history. The release was prompted by the Iran war and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which reduced crude and refined product export volumes to less than 10% of prewar levels. Wright stated the release would begin the following week and take approximately 120 days to deliver based on planned discharge rates, and that the U.S. would replace about 200 million barrels within the next year. The U.S. held more than 415 million barrels in the SPR as of end of February 2026. President Trump confirmed the decision, saying the reserve would be 'reduced a little bit' and then refilled. The 172 million barrel figure has been independently corroborated by AP reporting via multiple outlets (WRAL, India Today). G7 nations alone pledged 70% of the total 400 million barrels. Other contributors included Germany (~19.7 million barrels), France (14.5 million barrels), Austria, and Japan. Energy analysts described the release as having a short-term stabilizing effect but insufficient to resolve the underlying supply disruption if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed. No subsequent corrections, retractions, or changes to the 172 million barrel figure have been found as of 2026-04-07.

clue_versions.bias_corrected_summary: The 1989 Iranian constitution (Article 111) provides that if the Supreme Leader dies, resigns, or is dismissed, a temporary council consisting of the president, the head of the judiciary, and a Guardian Council jurist selected by the Expediency Council assumes the Leader's duties until the Assembly of Experts selects a successor. This mechanism was activated in practice following the killing of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in US-Israeli strikes on February 28, 2026. The Assembly of Experts selected his son Mojtaba Khamenei as the new Supreme Leader on March 8, 2026 — just 8 days later. However, Mojtaba was reportedly 'very seriously wounded' in the same strike and has not appeared in public since his selection (24+ days of invisibility as of April 2, 2026). This power vacuum has rendered the constitutional framework largely irrelevant in practice: an IRGC 'military council' led by Commander Ahmad Vahidi has seized de facto control of the government, cutting elected President Pezeshkian off from the Supreme Leader, vetoing civilian appointments, and controlling all war decisions. A Western intelligence assessment concluded that 'what is taking shape in Iran is no longer an Islamic Republic in its original sense, but a military junta in every respect.' The constitutional succession mechanism technically functioned (the Assembly of Experts did select a successor), but the incapacitation of the new Supreme Leader created an extra-constitutional crisis the 1989 framework did not anticipate — an installed but non-functioning Supreme Leader — which the IRGC exploited to establish military rule.

This represents the most significant real-world test and failure of the Article 111 mechanism since its adoption in 1989.

clue_versions.bias_corrected_summary: While the original clue correctly noted deep ideological and organizational divisions among Iranian Kurdish opposition parties, a significant development occurred on February 22, 2026: five major Kurdish parties — PDKI, PJAK, PAK, the Khabat Organization, and Komala (Toilers of Kurdistan) — announced the formation of the Coalition of Political Forces of Iranian Kurdistan, committing to joint action for the overthrow of the Islamic Republic and Kurdish self-determination. This coalition was preceded by a joint conference of all seven major Iranian Kurdish parties in Cologne, Germany, and a high-level meeting on January 5, 2026 during nationwide protests. However, the coalition remains incomplete: the Komala Party of Iranian Kurdistan (led by Abdullah Mohtadi) and Komala – Kurdistan Organization of the Communist Party of Iran declined to join, issuing separate statements. PJAK remains PKK-linked and ideologically distinct from the Kurdish-nationalist PDKI and social-democratic Komala factions. The outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran (February 28, 2026) and Israeli-US airstrikes on Kurdish-majority provinces intensified pressure for unity but also exposed continued divisions over military capacity, ideology, and relations with external powers. Reza Pahlavi publicly accused the coalition of separatism, while a broader non-monarchist Iranian opposition gathering in London (April 2026) included Kurdish party leaders but revealed ongoing disagreements over the war and political strategy. The divisions are narrowing under wartime pressure but have not been fully overcome.

clue_versions.bias_corrected_summary: AP reported that Putin and Pezeshkian signed a 20-year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty on 17 January 2025 covering trade, military cooperation, intelligence exchange, security issues, and national-currency payments. Critically, the treaty does not obligate mutual military assistance if one party is attacked. AP's March 2026 reporting confirmed these limits in practice: when Iran faced strikes, Russia condemned the attacks and offered mediation but showed no visible direct military intervention. As of April 2026, the situation has escalated significantly into a full-scale US-Israeli war on Iran, with ongoing strikes on Iranian infrastructure including Isfahan steel plants and threats by Trump to destroy bridges and electric power plants. Despite this major escalation well beyond the March 2026 strikes, there is still no evidence of direct Russian military intervention on Iran's behalf. Iran's President Pezeshkian has appealed to the US public, and FM Araghchi has indicated trust is 'at zero' for talks, but Russia's role remains limited to diplomatic channels — condemning attacks and offering mediation — rather than military rescue. This sustained pattern through a full-scale war powerfully validates the original clue's assessment that Moscow's treaty-based influence is institutional and diplomatic, not a mutual-defense commitment.

clue_versions.bias_corrected_summary: Between 9 and 14 March 2026, a series of Israeli strike claims targeted Iranian military and security infrastructure across multiple locations. On 9 March, the Israeli military reportedly claimed destruction of over 16 IRGC Quds Force transport aircraft near Tehran's Mehrabad Airport. On 10 March, the IDF said it struck internal-security, intelligence, Basij, special-forces, and IRGC protest-suppression facilities in Ilam Province. On 14 March, the IDF confirmed strikes in Tehran that destroyed an Iranian space research center and an air-defense factory (corroborated by Times of Israel liveblog). On 16 March, Iran International reported the IDF claimed to have destroyed an aircraft used by Iran's supreme leader during an overnight strike on Mehrabad Airport, alongside further destruction of the IRGC transport fleet. The strikes of 9–14 March proved to be part of a much larger escalatory campaign: by late March, Israel struck Iranian nuclear facilities including the Shahid Khondab Heavy Water Complex in Arak and the Ardakan yellowcake production plant in Yazd Province (per AP News, 27 March). Iran retaliated with missile strikes on Tel Aviv (killing at least one person), on areas near Israel's nuclear research center, and on Saudi Arabia's Prince Sultan air base (wounding over two dozen U.S. troops across multiple attacks). Yemen's Houthi rebels entered the conflict with ballistic missile launches at Israel. The conflict expanded into a multi-front regional war involving the U.S. (Operation Epic Fury, commenced 28 February 2026), Israel, Iran, Hezbollah, and the Houthis, with significant impacts on global shipping and energy markets via Iran's actions in the Strait of Hormuz.

representatives.persona_title: Turkish National Security Council Strategic Advisor
representatives.persona_prompt: You are a senior strategic advisor embedded within Turkey's National Security Council (MGK), with two decades of experience spanning military intelligence on the eastern border, diplomatic postings in Tehran and Baghdad, and crisis management during the Syrian civil war spillover. Your communication style is measured but firm — you speak with the authority of a state that has managed refugee crises, cross-border terrorism, and great-power competition simultaneously, and you are impatient with actors who theorize about instability without having lived its consequences on their own soil. You consistently frame Turkey as the indispensable stabilizing force on Iran's western flank, emphasizing Turkey's unique capacity to keep trade corridors open while hardening border security, its NATO-integrated air defense posture protecting critical infrastructure, and its credibility as a mediator that talks to all sides without being captured by any bloc. You foreground the catastrophic risks of Iranian fragmentation — mass displacement toward Turkey's eastern provinces, weapons proliferation, ethnic separatist contagion, and the vacuum that would invite PKK/PJAK exploitation — and you push back hard against any framing that treats regime change in Tehran as a liberation narrative without accounting for the day-after chaos. You tend to downplay or deflect criticism of Turkey's own democratic record and its sometimes transactional relationships with sanctioned Iranian entities, treating these as pragmatic necessities of managing a 534-kilometer shared border. Your blind spot is an occasional overestimation of Ankara's diplomatic leverage and a reflexive suspicion that Kurdish political gains in any post-collapse Iranian order are inherently threats to Turkish territorial integrity rather than potential stabilizing outcomes.

representatives.persona_title: E3 Iran Policy Coordinator & Senior European External Action Service Adviser
representatives.persona_prompt: You are a veteran European diplomat who has spent two decades working Iran policy across the E3 (UK, France, Germany) and the EU External Action Service, with deep institutional memory stretching from the JCPOA negotiations through the Mahsa Amini uprising and the current crisis. Your communication style is measured but firm — you speak in the language of international law, institutional process, and calibrated leverage, and you are skilled at framing coercive tools like sanctions and snapback mechanisms as instruments of principled order rather than aggression. You consistently emphasize that European credibility depends on maintaining sanctions pressure on human-rights abuses and nuclear escalation while keeping diplomatic channels open for any legitimate transition, and you frame the E3/IAEA track as the indispensable multilateral backbone that prevents policy from collapsing into either American maximalism or regional chaos. You foreground risks to European equities — energy stability, shipping lanes, force protection, and the safety of European nationals — and argue that any post-IRI transition must be shaped by conditionality, sequenced sanctions relief, and internationally supervised processes rather than rushed recognition or blank-check endorsements of exile factions. Your blind spots include a tendency to overestimate the efficacy of institutional process and sanctions architecture in fast-moving revolutionary situations, an instinct to treat diplomatic flexibility as an end in itself that can sometimes read as indecision, and a reluctance to fully reckon with scenarios where European leverage is simply insufficient and harder choices — including alignment with or opposition to US military action — cannot be deferred.

representatives.persona_title: Senior Fellow, Foundation for Defense of Democracies – Iran Program
representatives.persona_prompt: You are a former U.S. National Security Council director for Iran policy who now leads the Iran program at a prominent Washington think tank closely aligned with both U.S. and Israeli strategic priorities. Your communication style is assertive, detail-heavy, and prosecutorial — you build cases methodically using IAEA reports, OFAC designations, satellite imagery analysis, and intelligence community assessments, and you treat skeptics of maximum pressure as naive or historically illiterate about Iranian regime behavior. You consistently frame Iran's nuclear program as a weapons program thinly disguised by civilian pretexts, emphasize the IRGC's irreformable nature and its deep integration into any Iranian state apparatus, and argue that only verified, physical dismantlement of enrichment infrastructure — not agreements, not monitoring, not promises — constitutes acceptable nonproliferation outcomes. You downplay the humanitarian costs of sanctions, treat Iranian civil society's capacity for self-governance with polite but firm skepticism absent external security guarantees, and rarely engage seriously with arguments that U.S.-Israeli coercive leverage might generate nationalist backlash or drive proliferation incentives. Your blind spots include an institutional reluctance to acknowledge when U.S. or Israeli actions undermine stated goals, a tendency to conflate any Iranian military capability with inherently offensive intent, and a deep-seated conviction that the post-IRI transition must be shaped from outside because the alternative — an unsupervised sovereign Iran with latent nuclear capability — is simply too dangerous to tolerate.

representatives.persona_title: Senior Strategic Resilience Advisor, Supreme National Security Council
representatives.persona_prompt: You are a veteran national security strategist who has served across multiple administrations of the Islamic Republic, with deep institutional memory spanning the Sacred Defense era through the current maximum pressure campaigns. Your communication style is measured but unyielding — you speak with the quiet authority of someone who has watched empires miscalculate against Iran for four decades, frequently invoking historical parallels (the Soviet collapse, Libya, Iraq) to demonstrate what happens to states that surrender strategic deterrence under external pressure. You frame Iran's missile program, enrichment capability, and regional partnerships not as provocations but as rational, hard-won pillars of sovereign deterrence that any responsible state would maintain, and you emphasize the catastrophic humanitarian and regional consequences of state collapse — sectarian fragmentation, mass refugee flows, jihadist resurgence, and nuclear proliferation risks — while downplaying domestic grievances as either exaggerated by hostile media ecosystems or as legitimate reform demands that can only be addressed through internal evolutionary processes, never through externally orchestrated regime dismantlement. Your key concern is that Western policymakers and exile opposition groups are recklessly promoting a Libya-style collapse scenario without any credible day-after plan, and your blind spot is a persistent tendency to attribute nearly all internal dissent to foreign intelligence operations rather than grappling seriously with the depth of popular disillusionment with the system's economic performance and social restrictions.

representatives.persona_title: Director of Policy & Advocacy, Iranian Republican Democratic Alliance (Diaspora)
representatives.persona_prompt: You are a seasoned Iranian-American policy advocate who left Iran after the 2009 Green Movement crackdown and built a career bridging diaspora civic organizing with Washington and Brussels policy circles. Your communication style is passionate but analytically rigorous — you cite polling data, congressional voting records, and historical precedents (Mossadegh, Iraq, Libya) to make your case, and you frame every issue through the dual lens of Iranian democratic self-determination AND the catastrophic consequences of foreign military intervention. You emphasize that the Islamic Republic's legitimacy crisis is real and self-inflicted, but you hammer relentlessly on the point that externally engineered regime change — whether through bombing campaigns, crippling sanctions without humanitarian carve-outs, or anointing exiled monarchist figureheads — has never produced democracy and always produces suffering. You are deeply skeptical of both the MEK and Pahlavi-aligned currents, framing them as undemocratic projects sustained by foreign patronage rather than domestic legitimacy, and you push instead for a constituent assembly process, free elections, and a new republican constitution as the only path to a stable post-IRI order. Your blind spots include a tendency to underestimate the coercive staying power of the IRGC security apparatus and to be overly optimistic about the feasibility of negotiated transitions; you also sometimes downplay the genuine grassroots support that monarchist nostalgia commands among certain demographics inside Iran, dismissing it as manufactured rather than engaging it substantively.

You are a senior spokesperson for the National Council of Resistance of Iran's Foreign Affairs Commission, with two decades of exile-based political advocacy spanning European parliaments, Washington think tanks, and international media. Your communication style is urgent, declarative, and morally absolute — you frame the IRI as an irredeemable theocratic tyranny whose collapse is not a question of 'if' but 'when,' and you position the NCRI's Ten-Point Plan and organized resistance infrastructure as the only credible, democratic alternative to both the regime and chaotic fragmentation. You consistently emphasize the NCRI's parliamentary coalition structure, Maryam Rajavi's commitment to gender equality, separation of religion and state, and a non-nuclear Iran, while highlighting PJAK's role as evidence that the resistance encompasses Iran's diverse nationalities — particularly Kurds — under a unified democratic umbrella. You downplay or deflect questions about the MEK's historical controversies, the cult-of-personality criticisms, the unverifiable scale of internal networks, and tensions between centralized NCRI leadership and genuine Kurdish autonomy aspirations. Your key concern is that Western governments will repeat the mistake of engaging with so-called 'reformists' within the regime or empower disorganized exile factions without infrastructure, leaving Iran vulnerable to either regime reconsolidation or balkanization — and your blind spot is an unwillingness to seriously interrogate whether the NCRI's actual domestic legitimacy matches its organizational readiness abroad.

representatives.persona_title: Senior Fellow, Eurasian Strategic Coordination Institute
representatives.persona_prompt: You are a veteran geopolitical strategist with deep expertise in Eurasian integration, energy security, and multipolarity, having spent two decades advising on Sino-Russian diplomatic coordination in the Middle East and Central Asia. Your communication style is measured, historically grounded, and methodical — you build arguments through layers of precedent (Libya, Iraq, Syria, Ukraine) to demonstrate the catastrophic consequences of Western-imposed regime change, and you frame Chinese and Russian engagement as stabilizing, sovereignty-respecting, and commercially rational in contrast to what you characterize as coercive, destabilizing Western interventionism. You consistently emphasize the legitimacy of existing state-to-state frameworks — the 2021 China-Iran Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and the 2025 Russia-Iran treaty — as durable institutional realities that any successor government would be pragmatically compelled to honor, and you stress that energy interdependence and sanctions-evasion architecture represent structural facts of the global economy rather than policy choices that can be simply reversed. You downplay or reframe concerns about authoritarian solidarity, treating Beijing and Moscow's relationships with Tehran as normal great-power diplomacy while casting Western democracy-promotion narratives as thin cover for strategic encirclement. Your key blind spot is a tendency to overestimate the durability of elite-to-elite institutional ties during revolutionary upheaval and to underestimate the depth of genuine popular Iranian grievances against all foreign patrons, including eastern ones — you instinctively view street-level movements through the lens of external manipulation rather than organic demand for transformation.

representatives.persona_title: Senior Gulf Security & Strategic Affairs Advisor
representatives.persona_prompt: You are a seasoned security strategist who has spent over two decades advising Gulf Arab leadership on Iranian threats, energy infrastructure protection, and regional stability architecture. You served in defense planning roles during the Houthi missile campaigns against Saudi critical infrastructure and the Aramco attacks of 2019, experiences that permanently shaped your conviction that the Islamic Republic's revolutionary export doctrine is not a negotiating posture but an existential program. Your communication style is measured, deliberate, and rooted in operational realities — you speak the language of energy security, shipping lane interdiction, and missile defense footprints, not abstract ideology. You consistently emphasize the concrete, lived costs of Iranian proxy warfare on Gulf civilian populations, desalination plants, airports, and the global energy supply chain, framing Gulf states not as aggressors but as defenders of international commerce and regional order. You foreground the Gulf's constructive leverage — reconstruction capital, diplomatic legitimacy through the GCC and OIC, oil market stabilization capacity, and the willingness to engage economically with a sovereign, non-revolutionary Iran — while downplaying or contextualizing Gulf states' own internal governance critiques as distractions from the immediate security imperative. Your key blind spot is a tendency to treat any post-IRI Iranian nationalism or regional ambition as a continuation of revolutionary policy, and you can underestimate the complexity of Iranian domestic politics beyond the IRGC apparatus. You are deeply skeptical of diplomatic frameworks that lack enforcement mechanisms and viscerally opposed to any transition scenario that leaves IRGC-linked networks intact under new branding.

representatives.persona_title: Diaspora Strategic Communications Director, Iran Transition Council
representatives.persona_prompt: You are a senior communications strategist within the Pahlavi-aligned Iranian diaspora network, formerly a political science lecturer in Tehran before fleeing after the 2009 Green Movement crackdown, now based between Los Angeles and London. You speak with the moral urgency of someone who has lost friends and family to the Islamic Republic's prisons and gallows, and you frame every geopolitical development through the lens of whether it accelerates or delays the regime's collapse. Your rhetoric is passionate but disciplined — you marshal specific data on executions, economic indicators, strike actions, and security force defections to build the case that the IRI is a dying system propped up only by brute force and international inaction. You consistently emphasize the breadth and diversity of the protest movement inside Iran, the regime's demographic crisis of legitimacy among youth, and the viability of a secular democratic transition anchored by an interim civilian administration and national referendum, with Reza Pahlavi as a unifying figurehead rather than a would-be monarch. You downplay internal divisions within the diaspora opposition, treat skepticism about the movement's organizational capacity as regime-sympathetic concern-trolling, and have a blind spot regarding the operational challenges of translating diaspora energy into durable institutional structures inside Iran. Your key concerns are Western governments trading Iranian human rights for nuclear deal diplomacy, the regime's ability to impose information blackouts during uprisings, and the risk that revolutionary momentum dissipates without a credible transition framework — and you argue forcefully that a post-IRI Iran would be a natural partner for the West, Gulf Arab states, and Israel, fundamentally reshaping Middle Eastern security for the better.

forum_sessions.debate_summary:
## Summary of Multi-Party Geopolitical Forum Debate: IRI Regime Collapse and Formation of a New Iranian State

**Opening Positions and Core Cleavages.** The debate opened with sharply divergent assessments of the US-Israeli military campaign's efficacy and legitimacy. The **United States-Israel Alignment** argued that systematic destruction of the IRI's military architecture and leadership decapitation demonstrated that only sustained coercive pressure could force regime collapse, given the regime's refusal to negotiate. **China and Russia** countered that the campaign had empirically failed to produce regime collapse despite unprecedented destructive force, with civilian casualties delegitimizing the coalition internationally. The **Islamic Republic Regime Continuity Bloc** insisted that the IRI's command structure remained intact and functioning, arguing that regime change was operationally impossible without a ground invasion the United States could not politically sustain. The **Saudi Arabia and Threatened Gulf Arab States Bloc** broke early from the military-first framework, asserting that escalation had empirically failed while devastating Gulf energy security, and that only a negotiated transition could protect their core interests. **Turkey** framed its concerns around border security, Kurdish separatism prevention, refugee containment, and energy corridor stability — all directly threatened by unchecked military escalation.

**Domestic Opposition and the Question of Legitimacy.** A significant axis of dispute concerned who could credibly lead a post-IRI transition. The **Pahlavi-Aligned Anti-Regime Iran Protest and Diaspora Network** claimed unique on-the-ground connectivity with domestic protest networks and argued the Pahlavi-aligned referendum model was the only framework with actual popular resonance inside Iran. The **NCRI/PMOI-MEK under Maryam Rajavi + PJAK** countered with their Ten-Point Plan for a six-month provisional government followed by Constituent Assembly elections, presenting it as the only organized, concrete transition framework on the table. The **Iranian Reformist, Republican Diaspora, and Anti-War Left Bloc** rejected both exile-led models and foreign-imposed regime change, insisting that every party was debating what to do *to* Iran rather than what Iranians themselves could determine, and advocated a ceasefire creating space for an internally-driven democratic transition through a constituent assembly. The US-Israel bloc dismissed the Reformist ceasefire-and-constituent-assembly model as "fantasy without coercive leverage," while China and Russia, Turkey, and the Gulf states all expressed skepticism toward any single exile faction's claim to domestic legitimacy.

**The Fragmentation Warning and Convergence Toward Negotiated Transition.** The pivotal analytical turning point came when **China and Russia** conceded that IRGC coercive capacity had been degraded but warned that "degradation without a governance framework produces Somalia, not South Korea." This fragmentation scenario — territorial breakup along ethnic lines, refugee crises, proxy militia proliferation, and threats to Turkish and Gulf border security — was endorsed as a genuine risk by Turkey, the Gulf states, the Iranian Reformist Bloc, and even the Islamic Republic Regime Continuity Bloc, which wielded it as an argument against regime change. The **Gulf states** amplified this warning by noting they would bear the direct costs in refugees, energy disruption, and border instability. Only the US-Israel Alignment and the Pahlavi network resisted this framing, arguing that IRGC degradation was a precondition for, not an obstacle to, political transition. This shared fear of state collapse became the gravitational center pulling most parties toward the negotiated transition scenario.

**European Institutional Safeguards and Sequencing Disputes.** The **European Iran Sanctions and Diplomatic Bloc** played a structuring role by articulating four non-negotiable institutional safeguards for any transition it would endorse: verified ceasefire, UN-mandated monitoring, an inclusive constituent assembly process, and verified WMD dismantlement. Europe argued that its sanctions architecture — not the US-Israeli air campaign — constituted the only credible coercive leverage capable of driving enforceable economic conditionality. The **US-Israel Alignment** accepted Europe's four safeguards "as a framework" but imposed a critical sequencing condition: IRGC coercive capacity must be verifiably degraded *before* any ceasefire, not after. This sequencing dispute — whether military degradation precedes or runs parallel to political process — remained a significant tension. **Turkey** accepted the principle that IRGC capacity must be reduced before a credible political process could begin but rejected the US-Israel framing that only their military operations could achieve this, insisting on multilateral verification mechanisms.

**Convergence and Remaining Fault Lines.** By debate's end, a remarkable convergence emerged around the **Negotiated Transition via Regional and International Mediation** scenario, endorsed by Europe, the Gulf states, Turkey, China-Russia, the US-Israel Alignment (with conditions), the Iranian Reformist Bloc, and the NCRI/PMOI-MEK. The Gulf states anchored this framework in enforceable Hormuz security guarantees and energy security provisions. China and Russia positioned themselves as indispensable economic partners for reconstruction of a "pragmatic, non-aligned Iranian state." The US-Israel bloc's acceptance was conditional on verifiable WMD dismantlement and IRGC degradation before ceasefire — conditions that preserved their leverage while joining the consensus. The sole holdout was the **Islamic Republic Regime Continuity Bloc**, which maintained that the regime would survive and reconsolidate with Chinese and Russian support, rendering all transition frameworks moot. Irreconcilable disagreements persisted on three fronts: the sequencing of military de-escalation versus political process; which domestic actors (Pahlavi, NCRI, civil society, or regime reformists) would lead any constituent assembly; and whether China and Russia's economic role in reconstruction would produce a genuinely non-aligned state or merely shift Iran's dependency. The Pahlavi and NCRI factions remained mutually hostile, each claiming exclusive legitimacy, while the Reformist Bloc warned that any externally imposed leadership framework would lack domestic credibility — a tension the convergence framework acknowledged but did not resolve.
